## ASDA \#1: Blood RNAs for Febrile Illness Diagnosis

* Scoping review identified 286 RNA signatures from literature

* Signatures diagnose or predict outcomes of febrile illnesses (sepsis, TB, infections)

* Goal: Characterize and understand potential sources of biases

* Meta-analysis across many different studies

## ASDA \#2: `Breath print` for Lung Cancer Detection

* Breath samples from 500+ participants (lung cancer vs. healthy controls)

* Volatile organic compounds (VOCs) analyzed via mass spectrometry

* High-dimensional data: ~500-1500 compounds per sample

* Goal: Build analysis pipeline for biomarker discovery and classification


## Learning objectives of RNA-seq analysis

:::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=.45}

How do we get sequencing data?

\vspace{0.5cm}

* High-throughput sequencing data
  - data generation scheme
  - quantification

* Data normalization
  - intrinsic biases
  - gene-level adjustment
  - gene and sample adjustment

* Over-dispersed nature
  - count data
  - transformation

:::
::: {.column width=.45}

**How can we fit a model to sequencing data?**

* Linear modelling
  - a Gaussian linear model
  - a generalized linear model

* Multivariate linear models
  - a column space view

* Model-based inference
  - maximum likelihood learning
  - parametric inference

* Revisit RNA-seq
  - \textcolor{blue}{\texttt{\textbf{DESeq2}}} vs. \textcolor{blue}{\texttt{\textbf{limma-voom}}}
  - modelling and estimation

:::
::::::

## Key question: multiple sources of variation

- Can we identify multiple independent disease mechanisms?

- How do they manifest in observed transcriptional profiles?

\vspace{0.3cm}

1. **ER status**: Tumor-intrinsic differences (ER+ vs ER-)
2. **Age**: age effects in general population
3. **Menopause**: pre- vs. post-menopause

\vspace{0.3cm}

They are all correlated... but not necessarily the same

* Post-menopausal but young (e.g., surgical menopause)
* Pre-menopausal but older (late menopause)

## From `lect03`: Describe your model by stitching together random variables

\Large

Represent joint probability distributions using graphs

\normalsize

\vfill

:::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=.45}

**Nodes** = Random variables

* Observed (shaded)
* Latent/hidden (open)
* Parameters (dots or small nodes)

:::
::: {.column width=.45}

**Edges** = Dependencies

* Arrow $\rightarrow$ = causal/generative direction
* No arrow = correlation/association

:::
::::::


## Overall graphical model

:::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=.55}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[
    node distance=1.5cm,
    observed/.style={circle, draw, fill=gray!15, minimum size=1cm}
]
\node[observed] (age) {Age};
\node[observed, right=2.5cm of age] (meno) {Meno};
\node[observed, below=2cm of age] (er) {ER};
\node[observed, below=2cm of meno] (expr) {$Y_{g}$};

\draw[->, thick] (age) -- (meno);
\draw[->, thick] (age) -- (er);
\draw[->, thick] (meno) to[bend right=20] (er);
\draw[->, thick] (meno) -- node[right] {$\beta$} (expr);
\draw[->, thick] (er) -- node[below] {$\mu$} (expr);
\draw[->, thick] (age) to[bend right=20] node[right] {$\alpha$} (expr);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}

:::
::: {.column width=.45}

**Observed** variables:

* Age (continuous), Menopause (categorical), ER status (categorical)

* Gene expression matrix $Y_{ig}$ for a gene $g$ in a sample $i$.

\vspace{0.3cm}

**Parameters** (open):

* $\mu$: ER status effect
* $\alpha$: direct age effect
* $\beta$: menopause effect

:::
::::::

## TCGA BRCA data from `recount3`

We will use The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) breast cancer data

```{r download-data}
data.dir <- "../data/recount3"
dir.create(data.dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
.file <- file.path(data.dir, "tcga_brca_rse.rds")

if.needed(.file, {
    tcga.proj <- subset(available_projects(),
                        file_source == "tcga")
    brca.info <- tcga.proj[tcga.proj$project == "BRCA", ]
    rse.brca <- create_rse(brca.info)
    saveRDS(rse.brca, .file)
})
rse <- readRDS(.file)
```

## A probabilistic model on gene expression $Y$

:::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=.45}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[
    node distance=1.5cm,
    observed/.style={circle, draw, fill=gray!15, minimum size=1.3cm}
]
\node[observed] (age) {Age};
\node[observed, below=1.5cm of age] (meno) {Meno};
\node[observed, below=1.5cm of meno] (er) {ER};
\node[observed, right=2.5cm of meno] (expr) {$Y_{g}$};

\draw[->, thick] (age) -- node[above] {$\beta_1$} (expr);
\draw[->, thick] (meno) -- node[above] {$\beta_2$} (expr);
\draw[->, thick] (er) -- node[below] {$\beta_3$} (expr);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}

:::
::: {.column width=.55}

**Linear model for gene $g$:**

$$Y_{ig} = \beta_{1g} \cdot X_{i1} + \beta_{2g} \cdot X_{i2} + \beta_{3g} \cdot X_{i3} + \epsilon_{ig}$$

where $\epsilon_{ig} \sim N(0, \sigma^2_g)$

\vspace{0.3cm}

* $X_{i1}$: Age for individual $i$
* $X_{i2}$: Menopause status for individual $i$
* $X_{i3}$: ER status for individual $i$
* $\beta_{1g}, \beta_{2g}, \beta_{3g}$: Coefficients for gene $g$

:::
::::::

## Encoding categorical variables

**Categorical variables** need to be converted to numbers for the linear model

\vspace{0.5cm}

:::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=.48}

**Menopause status** ($X_{i2}$):

* Pre-menopause: $X_{i2} = 0$
* Post-menopause: $X_{i2} = 1$

:::
::: {.column width=.48}

**ER status** ($X_{i3}$):

* ER+: $X_{i3} = 0$
* ER-: $X_{i3} = 1$

:::
::::::

\vspace{0.5cm}

**Interpretation:** The coefficient represents the **difference** in expression between the two groups

* $\beta_{2g}$: Post-menopause vs. Pre-menopause difference for gene $g$
* $\beta_{3g}$: ER- vs. ER+ difference for gene $g$

## More explicit about the parameters

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[
    scale=1.8,
    node distance=1.5cm,
    observed/.style={circle, draw, fill=gray!15, minimum size=1.2cm, font=\large},
    param/.style={circle, draw, fill=white, minimum size=1cm, font=\large},
    plate/.style={draw, rectangle, rounded corners, inner sep=12pt, thick}
]

% Plate for individuals
\node[observed] (x1) at (-1, 1.5) {$X_{i1}$};
\node[observed] (x2) at (0, 1.5) {$X_{i2}$};
\node[observed] (x3) at (1, 1.5) {$X_{i3}$};
\node[observed] (y) at (0, 0) {$Y_{ig}$};

% Draw plate
\node[plate, fit=(x1)(x2)(x3)(y)] (plate1) {};
\node[font=\normalsize, anchor=south east] at (plate1.south east) {$i=1,\ldots,n$};

% Parameters (on the right)
\node[param] (beta1) at (3, 1.2) {$\beta_{1g}$};
\node[param] (beta2) at (3, 0.3) {$\beta_{2g}$};
\node[param] (beta3) at (3, -0.6) {$\beta_{3g}$};

% Arrows from parameters to Y
\draw[->, thick] (beta1) -- (y);
\draw[->, thick] (beta2) -- (y);
\draw[->, thick] (beta3) -- (y);

% Arrows from covariates to Y
\draw[->, thick] (x1) -- (y);
\draw[->, thick] (x2) -- (y);
\draw[->, thick] (x3) -- (y);

\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}

## We can write it down as a linear equation

\large

If it is deterministic and linear:

$$Y_{ig} = X_{i1} \beta_{1g} + X_{i2} \beta_{2g} + X_{i3} \beta_{3g}$$

* Are we treating $Y$ as a random variable?

* If not, what should we do?

\normalsize

## Adding uncertainty to the linear equations

\large

If it is stochastic and linear:

$$Y_{ig} = X_{i1} \beta_{1g} + X_{i2} \beta_{2g} + X_{i3} \beta_{3g} + \epsilon_{ig}$$

* What could be the distribution of $\epsilon$?

* Can we have a single $\epsilon$, namely $\epsilon_{ig} = \epsilon^{\star}$ for all $i$ and $g$?

\normalsize

## Building the response vector $\mathbf{y}_g$

For a single gene $g$, the response vector contains expression values across all $n$ samples:

$$\mathbf{y}_g = \begin{pmatrix} Y_{g1} \\ Y_{g2} \\ \vdots \\ Y_{gn} \end{pmatrix}$$

## Example: For a gene in our TCGA BRCA dataset:

```{r}
rowData(rse)[17709, 1:5]      # gene name etc.
yy <- raw.counts[17709, ]  # Extract some gene
head(yy, 10)               # Show first 10 values
```

Each entry $Y_{ig}$ represents the expression (read count) of gene $g$ in sample $i$

## Building the design matrix $\mathbf{X}$

The design matrix encodes our covariates (predictors) for all $n$ samples:

$$\mathbf{X} = \begin{pmatrix}
1 & X_{11} & X_{12} & X_{13} \\
1 & X_{21} & X_{22} & X_{23} \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\
1 & X_{n1} & X_{n2} & X_{n3}
\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}
1 & \text{Age}_1 & \text{Meno}_1 & \text{ER}_1 \\
1 & \text{Age}_2 & \text{Meno}_2 & \text{ER}_2 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\
1 & \text{Age}_n & \text{Meno}_n & \text{ER}_n
\end{pmatrix}$$

\vfill

What is the first column?

## TCGA metadata has very long factor names

```{r size="tiny", echo=FALSE}
temp_data <- colData(rse) %>% as.data.frame()
cat("Menopause status levels:\n")
unique(temp_data$tcga.xml_menopause_status)[1:3]
```

**Original names are too verbose for analysis!**

We need to shorten them for readability and modeling

## Factor name abbreviations we'll use

| Variable | Original | Shortened |
|----------|----------|-----------|
| **Menopause** | "Pre (<6 months since LMP...)" | "Pre" |
| | "Post (prior Bilateral...)" | "Post" |
| | "Peri (6-12 months...)" | "Peri" |
| **ER status** | "Positive" | "Positive" |
| | "Negative" | "Negative" |
| **Sample type** | "Primary Tumor" | "Tumor" |
| | "Solid Tissue Normal" | "Normal" |

## Example: Building $\mathbf{X}$ from TCGA metadata

```{r size="small"}
clinical.data <-
    colData(rse) %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    select(
        sample.id = tcga.tcga_barcode,
        sample.type = tcga.cgc_sample_sample_type,
        age = tcga.gdc_cases.diagnoses.age_at_diagnosis,
        menopause = tcga.xml_menopause_status,
        tumor.stage = tcga.gdc_cases.diagnoses.tumor_stage,
        ER.status = tcga.xml_breast_carcinoma_estrogen_receptor_status,
        PR.status = tcga.xml_breast_carcinoma_progesterone_receptor_status,
        HER2.status = tcga.xml_lab_proc_her2_neu_immunohistochemistry_receptor_status
    ) %>%
    mutate(
        # Shorten menopause status
        menopause = case_when(
            grepl("Pre", menopause) ~ "Pre",
            grepl("Post", menopause) ~ "Post",
            grepl("Peri", menopause) ~ "Peri",
            TRUE ~ menopause
        ),
        # Shorten sample type
        sample.type = case_when(
            grepl("Primary", sample.type) ~ "Tumor",
            grepl("Normal", sample.type) ~ "Normal",
            TRUE ~ sample.type
        )
    ) %>%
    as.data.table()
```

## Header lines of sample/clinical data

```{r size="tiny"}
head(clinical.data, 5)
```

## A handy function to build a design matrix

```{r}
X <- model.matrix(~ age + menopause + ER.status,
                  data = clinical.data)
head(X, 3)
```

## Let's write down this linear model in a matrix form

\large

$$\mathbf{y}_g = \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\beta}_g + \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_g$$

\normalsize

where:

:::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=.48}

\small

* $\mathbf{y}_g = \begin{pmatrix} Y_{g1} \\ Y_{g2} \\ \vdots \\ Y_{gn} \end{pmatrix}$ expression values

* $\mathbf{X} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & X_{11} & X_{12} & X_{13} \\ 1 & X_{21} & X_{22} & X_{23} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\ 1 & X_{n1} & X_{n2} & X_{n3} \end{pmatrix}$

\normalsize

:::
::: {.column width=.48}

\small

* $\boldsymbol{\beta}_g = \begin{pmatrix} \beta_{0g} \\ \beta_{1g} \\ \beta_{2g} \\ \beta_{3g} \end{pmatrix}$ coefficients

* $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_g = \begin{pmatrix} \epsilon_{1g} \\ \epsilon_{2g} \\ \vdots \\ \epsilon_{ng} \end{pmatrix}$ errors

\normalsize

:::
::::::

## Recap of `lect02` matrix algebra...

\large

Why is it useful to write them down in matrix?

\normalsize

## A design matrix = a column space view

We can rewrite the linear model as:

$$\mathbf{y}_g = \beta_{0g} \mathbf{x}_0 + \beta_{1g} \mathbf{x}_1 + \beta_{2g} \mathbf{x}_2 + \beta_{3g} \mathbf{x}_3 + \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_g$$

where $\mathbf{x}_j$ is the $j$-th column of $\mathbf{X}$

\onslide<2>{

\textbf{\color{teal} What is a linear regression?}

Finding the "best" \textbf{\color{teal} linear combination} of {\color{magenta} column vectors} to approximate $\mathbf{y}_g$

* Each column $\mathbf{x}_j$ represents a covariate pattern across all samples
* The coefficients $\beta_{jg}$ tell us how much each pattern contributes
* The fitted values $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_g = \mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_g$ lie in the \textbf{\color{magenta} column space} of $\mathbf{X}$

}

## Side: geometric intuition of column space (`lect09`)

If the whole prediction space can be made up by a linear combination of two $n$ vectors $\mathbf{x}_{1}$ and $\mathbf{x}_{2}$...

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=1.]
% Column space plane
\fill[blue!10] (-2,-1) -- (2,-1) -- (2.5,2) -- (-1.5,2) -- cycle;
\node at (5, 1.5) {\small Column space of $\mathbf{X} = [\mathbf{x}_{1}, \mathbf{x}_{2}]$};

% Vectors
\draw[->, thick, blue] (0,0) -- (1.5, 0.5) node[below right] {$\mathbf{x}_1$};
\draw[->, thick, blue] (0,0) -- (0.2, 1.5) node[above left] {$\mathbf{x}_2$};
\draw[->, thick, red] (0,0) -- (1.2, 1.8) node[right] {$\hat{\mathbf{y}}_g$};
\draw[->, thick, black] (0,0) -- (0.8, 2.5) node[above] {$\mathbf{y}_g$};

% Residual
\draw[dashed, thick, gray] (0.8, 2.5) -- (1.2, 1.8);
\node[right] at (1.0, 2.15) {$\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_g$};

% Origin
\fill (0,0) circle (0.05);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}

$\hat{\mathbf{y}}_g$ is the **projection** of $\mathbf{y}_g$ onto the column space of $\mathbf{X}$

## What have we missed?

\huge

$$\mathbf{y}_g = \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\beta}_g + \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_g$$

\onslide<2>{

\normalsize

We can assume/model:

\huge

$$\epsilon_{ig} \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(0, \sigma^{2}\right)$$

}

\normalsize

## How can we estimate the coefficients?

Use standard linear regression (`lm`) to estimate $\boldsymbol{\beta}_g$:

```{r}
y_gene <- log1p(raw.counts[17709, ]) # Take expression from gene 17709

fit <- lm(y_gene ~ age + menopause + ER.status, # Fit a linear model
          data = clinical.data)

summary(fit)$coefficients # View coefficients
```

## A better way to estimate: use `limma`

:::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=.3}

![](img/limma.png)

:::
::: {.column width=.6}
	
```{r eval=F, size="huge"}
library(limma)
```

:::
::::::

## `limma` can estimate the parameters across all the genes

```{r size="small"}
complete_samples <- complete.cases(clinical.data)
Y_filtered <- log1p(raw.counts[, complete_samples])
design <- model.matrix(~ age + menopause + ER.status,
                       data = clinical.data[complete_samples, ])

fit_limma <- lmFit(Y_filtered, design) # Fit linear models for all genes

fit_limma$coefficients[17709, ] # View coefficients for gene 17709
```

## Getting the top genes with `topTable`

After fitting, use empirical Bayes moderation and extract top genes:

```{r size="small"}
fit_limma <- eBayes(fit_limma) # Empirical Bayes of standard errors

top_genes <- topTable(fit_limma, coef = "ER.statusPositive",
                      number = 10, sort.by = "P")
top_genes[, c("logFC", "AveExpr", "t", "P.Value", "adj.P.Val")]
```

## `topTable` ranks genes by statistical significance with:

* `logFC`: log fold change
* `P.Value`: p-value
* `adj.P.Val`: adjusted p-value (FDR correction)

## What is `eBayes`?

**Empirical Bayes (EB)** moderation of variance estimates

\vspace{0.3cm}

**The problem:** With small sample sizes, gene-specific variance estimates $\hat{\sigma}^2_g$ are unreliable

* Some genes appear significant just by chance (unstable variance estimates)
* Leads to false discoveries

\vspace{0.3cm}

**The solution:** Borrow information across genes

* Assume all genes share similar variance structure
* Shrink each gene's variance toward a common prior distribution
* Results in more stable, moderated variance estimates

## Empirical Bayes on what?

`eBayes` moderates the **variance** (or standard error) estimates:

$$\tilde{\sigma}^2_g = \text{shrink}\left(\hat{\sigma}^2_g \text{ toward prior}\right)$$

\vspace{0.3cm}

**Without eBayes:** Each gene uses only its own data

* $\hat{\sigma}^2_g$ based on $n$ samples for gene $g$ alone
* Unstable when $n$ is small

**With eBayes:** Each gene borrows strength from all genes

* Pools information across $G$ genes to estimate prior distribution
* Shrinks extreme variance estimates toward the middle
* More stable t-statistics and p-values

## Why is eBayes useful for many genes?

:::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=.48}

**Traditional approach** (gene by gene):

* Fit model separately for each gene
* Each has independent $\hat{\sigma}^2_g$
* High variance in estimates
* Many false positives/negatives

:::
::: {.column width=.48}

**Empirical Bayes** (sharing information):

* Fit models for all genes
* Moderate all $\hat{\sigma}^2_g$ together
* Stable variance estimates
* Better statistical power
* Reduced false discoveries

:::
::::::

\vspace{0.3cm}

**Key insight:** With thousands of genes, we can learn a prior distribution from the data itself, then use it to improve individual gene estimates


## Why use `limma` instead of regular `lm`?

* **Borrows information** from all genes to get a better estimate of the variance (especially in smaller sample size settings)

* Efficiently fits many regression models **without replicating unnecessary calculations**!

* Arranges output in a convenient way to ease further analysis, visualization, and interpretation


## Genome-wide OLS fits

* Gene by gene:

  * `lm(y ~ x, data = gene)` for each gene

* All genes at once, using `limma`: 

  * `lmFit(object, design)`
  
  * `object` matrix-like object with expression values for all genes
  
  * `design` is a specially formatted design matrix (more on this later)
  
  * Note that `object` can be a Bioconductor container, such as an [`ExpressionSet`](https://kasperdanielhansen.github.io/genbioconductor/html/ExpressionSet.html) object

# Statistical inference for linear regression

## Recall: Linear model in matrix form

\Large

$$\mathbf{y}_g = \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\beta}_g + \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_g$$

\normalsize

where:

\large

:::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=.48}


* $\mathbf{y}_g \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$: expressions for gene $g$

* $\mathbf{\color{magenta} X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}$: design matrix (the same for all the genes)

:::
::: {.column width=.48}

* $\boldsymbol{\beta}_g \in \mathbb{R}^{p}$: coefficients for gene $g$

* $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_g \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$: error terms

:::
::::::

\normalsize

## Probabilistic model for each sample

For each sample $i$ and gene $g$:

$$Y_{ig} = \mathbf{x}_i \boldsymbol{\beta}_g + \epsilon_{ig}$$

where $\mathbf{x}_i$ is the $i$-th row of $\mathbf{X}$

**Assumption:** $\epsilon_{ig} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_g)$ independently

\vspace{0.5cm}

\onslide<2->{

$$Y_{ig} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i \boldsymbol{\beta}_g, \sigma^2_g)$$

}

## The probability density for each sample

$$p(Y_{ig} \mid \boldsymbol{\beta}_g, \sigma^2_g) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2_g}} \exp\left(-\frac{(Y_{ig} - \mathbf{x}_i \boldsymbol{\beta}_g)^2}{2\sigma^2_g}\right)$$


## Likelihood function

For all $n$ samples (assuming independence):

$$L(\boldsymbol{\beta}_g, \sigma^2_g \mid \mathbf{y}_g) = \prod_{i=1}^n p(Y_{ig} \mid \boldsymbol{\beta}_g, \sigma^2_g)$$

\onslide<2->{

\textbf{Log-likelihood:}

\begin{align*}
\ell(\boldsymbol{\beta}_g, \sigma^2_g) &= \sum_{i=1}^n \log p(Y_{ig} \mid \boldsymbol{\beta}_g, \sigma^2_g) \\
&= -\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi) - \frac{n}{2}\log(\sigma^2_g) - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2_g}\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_{ig} - \mathbf{x}_i \boldsymbol{\beta}_g)^2
\end{align*}

}

## Maximum likelihood estimation

To find $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_g$, maximize the log-likelihood:

$$\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_g = \arg\max_{\boldsymbol{\beta}_g} \ell(\boldsymbol{\beta}_g, \sigma^2_g)$$

\onslide<2->{

\textbf{Key observation:} Maximizing $\ell$ is equivalent to minimizing:

$$\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_{ig} - \mathbf{x}_i \boldsymbol{\beta}_g)^2 = (\mathbf{y}_g - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_g)^{\top}(\mathbf{y}_g - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_g)$$

}

\onslide<3->{

\begin{center}
\colorbox{yellow}{\textbf{Maximum Likelihood = Ordinary Least Squares!}}
\end{center}

Under Gaussian errors, MLE and OLS give the same coefficient estimates

}

## Ordinary Least Squares solution

Minimize $(\mathbf{y}_g - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_g)^{\top}(\mathbf{y}_g - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_g)$ with respect to $\boldsymbol{\beta}_g$

\vspace{0.3cm}

Take derivative and set to zero:

\begin{align*}
\frac{\partial}{\partial \boldsymbol{\beta}_g}\left[(\mathbf{y}_g - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_g)^{\top}(\mathbf{y}_g - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_g)\right] &= 0 \\
-2\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{y}_g + 2\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_g &= 0
\end{align*}

\vspace{0.3cm}

**OLS estimator:**

$$\boxed{\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_g = (\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{y}_g}$$

## Beyond point estimates: Uncertainty quantification

So far we have $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_g$ as a **point estimate**

\vspace{0.5cm}

**But we also need:**

* Standard errors for $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_g$
* Confidence intervals
* Hypothesis tests (p-values)

\vspace{0.5cm}

\onslide<2->{

\textbf{Key question:} What is the distribution of $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_g$?

Since $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_g$ depends on $\mathbf{y}_g$, and $\mathbf{y}_g$ is random, $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_g$ is also a random variable!

}

## Variance of the coefficient estimates

<!-- Since $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_g = (\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{y}_g$ and $\mathbf{y}_g = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_g + \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_g$: -->

\begin{align*}
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_g &= (\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^{\top}(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_g + \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_g) \\
&= \boldsymbol{\beta}_g + (\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_g
\end{align*}

\vspace{0.3cm}

\onslide<2->{

\textbf{Variance:}

$$\text{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_g) = \text{Var}[(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_g]$$

Since $\text{Var}(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_g) = \sigma^2_g \mathbf{I}$:

$$\boxed{\text{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_g) = \sigma^2_g (\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})^{-1}}$$

}

## Inference for coefficients

For the $j$-th coefficient of gene $g$:

$$\hat{\beta}_{jg} \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\beta_{jg}, \sigma^2_g [(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})^{-1}]_{jj}\right)$$

Standard error: $\text{SE}(\hat{\beta}_{jg}) = \hat{\sigma}_g \sqrt{[(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})^{-1}]_{jj}}$

\vspace{0.3cm}

**t-statistic for** $H_0: \beta_{jg} = 0$:

$$t_{jg} = \frac{\hat{\beta}_{jg}}{\text{SE}(\hat{\beta}_{jg})} \sim t_{n-p}$$


## Knowing the distribution each coefficient

\large

**t-statistic for** $H_0: \beta_{jg} = 0$:

$$t_{jg} = \frac{\hat{\beta}_{jg}}{\text{SE}(\hat{\beta}_{jg})} \sim t_{n-p}$$

This allows us to:

* Test significance of individual coefficients

* Construct confidence intervals

\normalsize

# Generalized linear models for RNA-seq

## Limitation of Gaussian linear models for count data

**Problem:** RNA-seq data are **counts**, not continuous values

:::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=.45}

**Gaussian assumption:**

* $Y_{ig} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_{ig}, \sigma^2_g)$
* Continuous values
* Can be negative
* Constant variance

:::
::: {.column width=.45}

**RNA-seq reality:**

* $Y_{ig} \in \{0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots\}$
* Discrete counts
* Non-negative integers
* Variance increases with mean (overdispersion)

:::
::::::

\vspace{0.5cm}

**Solution:** Generalized Linear Models (GLM) with appropriate distribution

## Negative Binomial for RNA-seq [@Anders2010-cf; @Robinson2008-pd]

$$Y_{ig} \sim \text{NB}(\mu_{ig}, \phi_g)$$

Where:

* $\mu_{ig}$: mean expression for gene $g$ in sample $i$
* $\phi_g$: dispersion parameter for gene $g$ (captures overdispersion)

\vspace{0.3cm}

**Key property:**

$$\mathbb{E}[Y_{ig}] = \mu_{ig}, \qquad \text{Var}(Y_{ig}) = \mu_{ig} + \phi_g \mu_{ig}^2$$

## Connecting covariates to the mean: log-link function

**Linear model (what we've been doing):**

$$\mu_{ig} = \mathbf{x}_i \boldsymbol{\beta}_g = \sum_{j} X_{ij} \beta_{jg}$$

\onslide<2->{

\vspace{0.5cm}

\textbf{GLM solution:} Use a \textbf{link function} to ensure $\mu_{ig} > 0$

$$\log(\mu_{ig}) = \mathbf{x}_i \boldsymbol{\beta}_g = \sum_{j} X_{ij} \beta_{jg}$$

}

\onslide<3->{

$$\boxed{\mu_{ig} = \exp\left(\sum_{j} X_{ij} \beta_{jg}\right) = \exp(\mathbf{x}_i \boldsymbol{\beta}_g)}$$

}

## GLM for RNA-seq: putting it together

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=1.0]
  % Parameters (to be estimated - open circles)
  \node[draw, circle, minimum size=1cm, fill=white] (beta) at (2, 5) {$\boldsymbol{\beta}_g$};
  \node[font=\small, above] at (2, 5.55) {coefficients};

  \node[draw, circle, minimum size=1cm, fill=white] (phi) at (6, 5) {$\phi_g$};
  \node[font=\small, above] at (6, 5.55) {dispersion};

  % Covariates (observed - filled circle)
  \node[draw, circle, minimum size=1cm, fill=green!20, thick] (X) at (0.5, 3.5) {$\mathbf{x}_i$};
  \node[font=\small, left] at (0, 3.5) {covariates};

  % Mean (derived)
  \node[draw, circle, minimum size=1cm, fill=white] (mu) at (4, 3.5) {$\mu_{ig}$};
  \node[font=\small, above right] at (4.6, 3.5) {mean};

  % Lambda (latent)
  \node[draw, circle, minimum size=1cm, fill=white, dashed, thick] (lambda) at (4, 1.8) {$\lambda_{ig}$};
  \node[font=\small, right] at (4.6, 1.8) {latent};

  % Y (observed)
  \node[draw, circle, minimum size=1cm, fill=blue!20, thick] (Y) at (4, 0.2) {$Y_{ig}$};
  \node[font=\small, below] at (4, -0.4) {count};

  % Arrows
  \draw[->, thick] (X) -- (mu);
  \draw[->, thick] (beta) -- (mu);
  \draw[->, thick, red] (2.7, 4.5) -- (3.2, 4.0) node[midway, above, font=\small] {log-link};
  \draw[->, thick] (mu) -- (lambda);
  \draw[->, thick] (phi) -- (lambda);
  \draw[->, thick] (lambda) -- (Y);

  % Equations
  \node[font=\normalsize, align=left, anchor=west] at (7, 3) {$\log(\mu_{ig}) = \mathbf{x}_i \boldsymbol{\beta}_g$};
  \node[font=\normalsize, align=left, anchor=west] at (7, 1.5) {$\lambda_{ig} \sim \text{Gamma}(\mu_{ig}, \phi_g)$};
  \node[font=\normalsize, align=left, anchor=west] at (7, 0.0) {$Y_{ig} | \lambda_{ig} \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_{ig})$};

  % Legend
  \draw[rounded corners, gray] (9.5, 5.5) rectangle (13, 3.8);

  \node[draw, circle, minimum size=0.45cm, fill=blue!20, thick] at (10, 5.2) {};
  \node[font=\small, right] at (10.3, 5.2) {observed};

  \node[draw, circle, minimum size=0.45cm, fill=white, dashed, thick] at (10, 4.7) {};
  \node[font=\small, right] at (10.3, 4.7) {latent};

  \node[draw, circle, minimum size=0.45cm, fill=white] at (10, 4.2) {};
  \node[font=\small, right] at (10.3, 4.2) {to be estimated};

\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}

## Interpretation of coefficients in GLM

In the log-link GLM:

$$\log(\mu_{ig}) = \beta_{0g} + \beta_{1g} X_{i1} + \beta_{2g} X_{i2} + \cdots$$

\vspace{0.3cm}

**Interpretation of $\beta_{jg}$:**

* $\beta_{jg}$: **log fold-change** in mean expression for a one-unit $\Delta$ in $X_{ij}$

\onslide<2->{

\vspace{0.3cm}

\textbf{Example:} If $\beta_{1g} = 0.693$ (for a binary treatment variable):

$$\mu_{ig}^{\text{treated}} = \mu_{ig}^{\text{control}} \times \exp(0.693) = \mu_{ig}^{\text{control}} \times 2$$

Treatment doubles the mean expression (2-fold change)

}

## Comparing Gaussian LM vs. GLM for RNA-seq

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\hline
& \textbf{Gaussian LM} & \textbf{NB GLM} \\
\hline
Distribution & $Y_{ig} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_{ig}, \sigma^2_g)$ & $Y_{ig} \sim \text{NB}(\mu_{ig}, \phi_g)$ \\
Mean model & $\mu_{ig} = \mathbf{x}_i \boldsymbol{\beta}_g$ & $\log(\mu_{ig}) = \mathbf{x}_i \boldsymbol{\beta}_g$ \\
Link function & Identity & Log \\
$\beta_{jg}$ interpretation & Additive effect & Log fold-change \\
Variance & Constant $\sigma^2_g$ & Increases with mean \\
Data type & Continuous & Count \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\vspace{0.5cm}

**For RNA-seq:** GLM with negative binomial distribution is more appropriate!

## `DESeq2` [@Love2014-dl] / `edgeR` [@Robinson2008-pd] directly model count data

1. Use negative binomial GLM
2. Estimate dispersion parameters
3. Perform inference on $\boldsymbol{\beta}_g$

## Example: `edgeR` for negative binomial GLM

```{r size="tiny", message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
.file <- file.path(data.dir, "edgeR_results.rds")
if.needed(.file, {
    # Create DGEList object with count data
    dge <- DGEList(counts = raw.counts[, complete_samples],
                   samples = clinical.data[complete_samples, ])

    # Normalize for library size differences
    dge <- calcNormFactors(dge)

    # Estimate dispersion (phi_g for each gene)
    dge <- estimateDisp(dge, design)

    # Fit negative binomial GLM
    QLfit <- glmQLFit(dge, design = design)

    # Test for ER status effect
    QLtest_ER <- glmQLFTest(QLfit, coef = "ER.statusPositive")

    saveRDS(QLtest_ER, .file)
})
QLtest_ER <- readRDS(.file)

topTags(QLtest_ER)[1:3, c("logFC", "logCPM", "PValue", "FDR")]
```

## Example: `DESeq2` for negative binomial GLM

```{r size="tiny", message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
.file <- file.path(data.dir, "deseq2_results.rds")
if.needed(.file, {
    # Create DESeqDataSet from count matrix
    dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(
        countData = raw.counts[, complete_samples],
        colData = clinical.data[complete_samples, ],
        design = ~ age + menopause + ER.status
    )

    # Run DESeq2 pipeline (normalization + dispersion + GLM)
    dds <- DESeq(dds, quiet = TRUE)

    # Extract results for ER status
    res_ER <- results(dds, name = "ER.status_Positive_vs_Negative")

    saveRDS(res_ER, .file)
})
res_ER <- readRDS(.file)

res_ER[order(res_ER$padj), ][1:3, c("log2FoldChange", "pvalue", "padj")]
```

## How `DESeq2` estimates dispersion parameter $\phi$

\large

**The challenge:** Estimating $\phi_g$ from small samples is unreliable

**DESeq2's solution:** Empirical Bayes shrinkage

1. Fit gene-wise dispersions (MLE)
2. Fit a trend: $\phi_g \sim f(\mu_g)$
3. Shrink toward the trend

## `DESeq2` dispersion estimates

```{r deseq2-dispersion, fig.height=2.8, fig.width=4, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
.file <- file.path(data.dir, "dds_full.rds")
if.needed(.file, {
    dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(
        countData = raw.counts[, complete_samples],
        colData = clinical.data[complete_samples, ],
        design = ~ age + menopause + ER.status
    )
    dds <- DESeq(dds, quiet = TRUE)
    saveRDS(dds, .file)
})
dds <- readRDS(.file)
```

```{r eval=F}
plotDispEsts(dds, main = "DESeq2 Dispersion Estimates")
```

## 

```{r deseq2-dispersion-plot, fig.height=3, fig.width=5, echo=F}
plotDispEsts(dds, main = "DESeq2 Dispersion Estimates")
```


# The limma-voom approach

## Two main approaches for RNA-seq differential expression

:::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=.48}

\centering
\includegraphics[height=1.8cm]{img/DESeq2.png}
\hspace{0.3cm}
\includegraphics[height=1.8cm]{img/edgeR.png}

**Count-based GLM**

* Model counts directly with NB
* Estimate dispersion $\phi_g$
* Use GLM framework

:::
::: {.column width=.48}

\centering
\includegraphics[height=2cm]{img/limma.png}

**Transformation + Linear Model**

* Transform counts to log-scale
* Apply weighted linear models
* Use **voom** for weights

:::
::::::

\vspace{0.5cm}

Both approaches give similar results in practice! But `DESeq2` is ...

## Mean-variance relationship and heteroskedasticity

:::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=.48}

```{r mv-raw, fig.height=2.8, fig.width=2.8, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
counts_sub <- raw.counts[, complete_samples]
mean_expr <- rowMeans(counts_sub)
var_expr <- rowVars(counts_sub)

data.frame(mean = log10(mean_expr + 1),
           var = log10(var_expr + 1)) %>%
    filter(is.finite(mean) & is.finite(var)) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = mean, y = var)) +
    ggrastr::rasterise(geom_point(alpha = 0.1, size = 0.5), dpi = 300) +
    geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
    labs(x = "log10(mean + 1)", y = "log10(variance + 1)",
         title = "Raw: Strong M-V trend") +
    theme_minimal()
```

:::
::: {.column width=.48}

```{r mv-log, fig.height=2.8, fig.width=2.8, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
log_counts <- log2(counts_sub + 1)
mean_log <- rowMeans(log_counts)
var_log <- rowVars(log_counts)

data.frame(mean = mean_log,
           var = sqrt(sqrt(var_log))) %>%
    filter(is.finite(mean) & is.finite(var)) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = mean, y = var)) +
    ggrastr::rasterise(geom_point(alpha = 0.1, size = 0.5), dpi = 300) +
    geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, color = "blue", span = 0.3) +
    labs(x = "Mean log2(count + 1)", y = "sqrt(SD)",
         title = "Log counts") +
    theme_minimal()
```

:::
::::::

## Why does heteroskedasticity matter?

**OLS assumes constant variance** (homoskedasticity)

\vspace{0.3cm}

:::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=.55}

When variance depends on mean:

* High-variance observations get **less weight** than they should
* Standard errors are **incorrect**
* t-statistics and **p-values are wrong**

\vspace{0.3cm}

For RNA-seq:

* Low-count genes have high variance
* They get inflated t-statistics
* **More false positives!**

:::
::: {.column width=.4}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.8]
% Axes
\draw[->] (0,0) -- (5,0) node[right] {Mean};
\draw[->] (0,0) -- (0,4) node[above] {Var};

% Curve showing increasing variance
\draw[thick, blue] (0.5,0.3) .. controls (2,1) and (3,2.5) .. (4.5,3.5);

% Points with error bars
\foreach \x/\y/\h in {1/0.5/0.3, 2/1.2/0.6, 3/2/1, 4/2.8/1.4} {
    \fill[red] (\x, \y) circle (2pt);
    \draw[red, thick] (\x, \y-\h*0.5) -- (\x, \y+\h*0.5);
}

\node[font=\small] at (2.5, -0.5) {Variance increases with mean};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}

:::
::::::

## The voom solution: Precision weights

**Key idea:** Model the mean-variance relationship, use it to weight observations

\vspace{0.3cm}

$$w_{ig} = \frac{1}{\text{Var}(Y_{ig})}$$

\vspace{0.3cm}

* Observations with **high variance** get **low weight**
* Observations with **low variance** get **high weight**
* Weights are estimated from the **mean-variance trend**

\vspace{0.3cm}

This is called **Weighted Least Squares (WLS)**

## Weighted Least Squares

**OLS solution:**

$$\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_g = (\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}_g$$

\vspace{0.5cm}

**WLS solution:**

$$\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_g = (\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{W}_g\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{W}_g\mathbf{y}_g$$

where $\mathbf{W}_g = \text{diag}(w_{1g}, w_{2g}, \ldots, w_{ng})$

\vspace{0.5cm}

**Intuition:** In minimizing RSS, put less weight on imprecise observations

$$\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_g = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \sum_{i=1}^n w_{ig}(Y_{ig} - \mathbf{x}_i\boldsymbol{\beta})^2$$

## The voom algorithm: Step by step

:::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=.55}

**Step 1:** Fit linear model to $\log_2(\text{CPM} + 0.5)$

**Step 2:** Extract residual standard deviations $s_g$

**Step 3:** Fit lowess curve to mean vs $\sqrt{s_g}$ trend

**Step 4:** Compute precision weights:
$$w_{ig} = \frac{1}{\hat{f}(\hat{\mu}_{ig})^4}$$

**Step 5:** Re-fit with weights using `lmFit`

**Step 6:** Apply `eBayes` for moderated t-statistics

:::
::: {.column width=.4}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.65,
    box/.style={rectangle, draw, rounded corners, minimum width=2.2cm, minimum height=0.7cm, font=\small}]

\node[box, fill=blue!20] (fit1) at (0, 6) {Fit LM};
\node[box, fill=green!20] (resid) at (0, 4.5) {Get residuals};
\node[box, fill=yellow!20] (lowess) at (0, 3) {Fit M-V trend};
\node[box, fill=orange!20] (weights) at (0, 1.5) {Calc weights};
\node[box, fill=red!20] (fit2) at (0, 0) {WLS + eBayes};

\draw[->, thick] (fit1) -- (resid);
\draw[->, thick] (resid) -- (lowess);
\draw[->, thick] (lowess) -- (weights);
\draw[->, thick] (weights) -- (fit2);

\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}

:::
::::::

## voom in action: TCGA BRCA data

```{r eval=F, size="normalsize"}
## just like edgeR
dge <- DGEList(counts = raw.counts[, complete_samples])
dge <- calcNormFactors(dge)

## VOOM transformation
voom_result <- voom(dge, design = design, plot = TRUE)
```

## voom in action: TCGA BRCA data

```{r voom-fit, fig.height=2.8, fig.width=5, fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, echo=F}
dge <- DGEList(counts = raw.counts[, complete_samples])
dge <- calcNormFactors(dge)
voom_result <- voom(dge, design = design, plot = TRUE) # VOOM!
```

## Understanding the voom plot

:::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=.48}

```{r voom-plot-explain, fig.height=2.8, fig.width=2.8, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
voom_result <- voom(dge, design = design, plot = TRUE)
```

:::
::: {.column width=.48}

**X-axis:** Average log-expression (mean of $\log_2$ CPM)

**Y-axis:** $\sqrt{\text{SD}}$ of residuals (quarter-root variance)

**Red curve:** Lowess fit to the trend

**Interpretation:**

* Downward trend = heteroskedasticity
* Low-expression genes have high variance
* Weights correct for this

:::
::::::

## Fitting the weighted linear model

```{r voom-limma-fit, size="scriptsize", message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Fit linear model with voom weights
fit_voom <- lmFit(voom_result, design)

# Apply empirical Bayes moderation
fit_voom <- eBayes(fit_voom)

# Get top genes for ER status
topTable(fit_voom, coef = "ER.statusPositive", number = 5)[,
    c("logFC", "AveExpr", "t", "P.Value", "adj.P.Val")]
```

## What are the voom weights?

```{r voom-weights, fig.height=2.8, fig.width=5.5, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Show distribution of weights
weights_df <- data.frame(
    weight = as.vector(voom_result$weights),
    mean_expr = rep(rowMeans(voom_result$E), ncol(voom_result$E))
)

p1 <- ggplot(weights_df, aes(x = weight)) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) +
    labs(x = "Voom weight", y = "Count", title = "Distribution of weights") +
    theme_minimal()

p2 <- weights_df %>%
    sample_n(10000) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = mean_expr, y = weight)) +
    ggrastr::rasterise(geom_point(alpha = 0.1, size = 0.5), dpi = 300) +
    geom_smooth(method = "loess", color = "red", se = FALSE) +
    labs(x = "Mean log2 expression", y = "Weight",
         title = "Weight vs Expression") +
    theme_minimal()

p1 + p2
```

Higher expression $\rightarrow$ higher weight (more precise)

## limma-voom vs limma-trend

:::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=.48}

**limma-voom**

* Weights at **observation** level
* Each sample-gene gets its own weight
* More flexible

```{r eval=FALSE}
voom_result <- voom(dge, design)
fit <- lmFit(voom_result, design)
fit <- eBayes(fit)
```

:::
::: {.column width=.48}

**limma-trend**

* Shrinkage at **gene** level
* Prior variance depends on mean expression
* Simpler, often sufficient

```{r eval=FALSE}
fit <- lmFit(logCPM, design)
fit <- eBayes(fit, trend = TRUE)
```

:::
::::::

\vspace{0.3cm}

**When to use which?**

* voom: When library sizes vary a lot
* trend: When library sizes are similar

## Comparing all three methods on TCGA BRCA

```{r method-comparison, fig.height=2.8, fig.width=6, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Get results from all methods
# limma-voom
pvals_voom <- topTable(fit_voom, coef = "ER.statusPositive",
                        number = Inf, sort.by = "none")$P.Value

# edgeR
pvals_edger <- QLtest_ER$table$PValue

# DESeq2
pvals_deseq2 <- res_ER$pvalue[match(rownames(QLtest_ER$table),
                                     rownames(res_ER))]

# Combine results
comparison_df <- data.frame(
    voom = -log10(pvals_voom),
    edgeR = -log10(pvals_edger[1:length(pvals_voom)]),
    DESeq2 = -log10(pvals_deseq2[1:length(pvals_voom)])
) %>%
    filter(is.finite(voom) & is.finite(edgeR) & is.finite(DESeq2))

p1 <- ggplot(comparison_df, aes(x = voom, y = edgeR)) +
    ggrastr::rasterise(geom_point(alpha = 0.1, size = 0.5), dpi = 300) +
    geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
    labs(x = "-log10(p) voom", y = "-log10(p) edgeR",
         title = "voom vs edgeR") +
    theme_minimal()

p2 <- ggplot(comparison_df, aes(x = voom, y = DESeq2)) +
    ggrastr::rasterise(geom_point(alpha = 0.1, size = 0.5), dpi = 300) +
    geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
    labs(x = "-log10(p) voom", y = "-log10(p) DESeq2",
         title = "voom vs DESeq2") +
    theme_minimal()

p3 <- ggplot(comparison_df, aes(x = edgeR, y = DESeq2)) +
    ggrastr::rasterise(geom_point(alpha = 0.1, size = 0.5), dpi = 300) +
    geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
    labs(x = "-log10(p) edgeR", y = "-log10(p) DESeq2",
         title = "edgeR vs DESeq2") +
    theme_minimal()

p1 + p2 + p3
```

**Methods agree well!** Especially for top-ranked genes

## Summary: When to use which method?

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\hline
& \textbf{limma-voom} & \textbf{DESeq2} & \textbf{edgeR} \\
\hline
Data type & Counts & Counts & Counts \\
Model & Weighted LM & NB GLM & NB GLM \\
M-V handling & voom weights & Dispersion & Dispersion \\
Speed & Fast & Moderate & Fast \\
Small samples & Good & Very good & Very good \\
Large samples & Very good & Good & Good \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\vspace{0.5cm}

**Practical advice:**

* All three methods are valid and well-tested
* For most datasets, results will be similar
* Use DESeq2/edgeR for small samples ($n < 10$ per group)
* Use limma-voom for large samples or when library sizes vary

## Key takeaways

1. **RNA-seq counts** have mean-variance relationship (heteroskedasticity)

2. **voom** estimates precision weights from M-V trend

3. **Weighted least squares** gives more accurate inference

4. **DESeq2/edgeR** model counts directly with negative binomial

5. **All methods** borrow information across genes (empirical Bayes)

6. **Results are similar** for well-powered studies
